chapter_title: Computer Awareness: Competitive Exams Complete Notes & Facts

notes_list.title: What is a Computer?
notes_list.basic_overview: A computer is an electronic programmable machine that accepts data as input, processes it according to instructions, stores data and produces meaningful output.
notes_list.extra_info_content: The basic functional cycle of a computer is Input → Processing → Output, with storage and control functions supporting the complete system. Competitive exams frequently ask the definition, characteristics and basic working cycle of a computer.

notes_list.title: Data vs Information
notes_list.basic_overview: Data refers to raw facts and figures, whereas information is processed and organized data that has meaningful context.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Example: 85, 90 and 75 are raw data. Their calculated average of 83.33, when interpreted as a student's performance, represents information.

notes_list.title: Characteristics of Computers
notes_list.basic_overview: Important characteristics of computers include high speed, accuracy, diligence, automation, versatility, large storage capacity and consistency.
notes_list.extra_info_content: A computer does not normally possess human-like intelligence or emotions by itself. Its output depends on the instructions, algorithms and data supplied to it.

notes_list.title: Limitations of Computers
notes_list.basic_overview: Computers have no inherent common sense, emotions or independent judgment and generally require instructions and valid data to perform tasks.
notes_list.extra_info_content: The phrase GIGO means Garbage In, Garbage Out. Incorrect or poor-quality input can produce incorrect or meaningless output even when the computer processes it correctly.

notes_list.title: First Generation Computers
notes_list.basic_overview: First-generation computers primarily used vacuum tubes for electronic circuitry and were generally large, expensive and power-hungry.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Typical examples associated with the first generation include ENIAC, EDVAC and UNIVAC-I. Machine language was central to programming in this era.

notes_list.title: Second Generation Computers
notes_list.basic_overview: Second-generation computers replaced vacuum tubes with transistors, making computers smaller, faster, more reliable and more energy efficient.
notes_list.extra_info_content: FORTRAN and COBOL became important high-level programming languages during this broad period.

notes_list.title: Third Generation Computers
notes_list.basic_overview: Third-generation computers used integrated circuits instead of individual transistors, improving reliability, speed and reducing physical size.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Operating systems and multiprogramming became increasingly important during this generation.

notes_list.title: Fourth Generation Computers
notes_list.basic_overview: Fourth-generation computers are associated with microprocessors and the rapid development of personal computers.
notes_list.extra_info_content: The microprocessor integrated major CPU functions onto a single chip, contributing to the development of compact and affordable computing systems.

notes_list.title: Fifth Generation Computers
notes_list.basic_overview: Fifth-generation computing is commonly associated with artificial intelligence, knowledge-based systems, natural language processing and advanced parallel processing.
notes_list.extra_info_content: The exact boundaries of computer generations are not universally fixed. In competitive-exam questions, fifth generation is commonly linked with AI and advanced computing.

notes_list.title: CPU
notes_list.basic_overview: CPU stands for Central Processing Unit and performs instruction execution and major processing operations in a computer.
notes_list.extra_info_content: CPU is commonly described through the Control Unit, Arithmetic Logic Unit and registers. Modern processors contain additional specialized units and multiple cores.

notes_list.title: ALU
notes_list.basic_overview: ALU stands for Arithmetic Logic Unit and performs arithmetic and logical operations.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Arithmetic operations include addition and subtraction, while logical operations include comparisons and Boolean operations such as AND, OR and NOT.

notes_list.title: Control Unit
notes_list.basic_overview: The Control Unit coordinates and directs the execution of instructions by controlling the flow of data and signals within the computer.
notes_list.extra_info_content: The Control Unit does not primarily perform arithmetic calculations. It interprets instructions and coordinates other components.

notes_list.title: Registers
notes_list.basic_overview: Registers are very small and very fast storage locations inside or closely associated with the CPU that temporarily hold data, instructions or addresses.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Examples include accumulator, program counter, instruction register, memory address register and memory data register. Exact register organization varies by processor architecture.

notes_list.title: Keyboard
notes_list.basic_overview: A keyboard is an input device used to enter text, numbers, commands and other characters into a computer.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Common keyboard keys include alphanumeric keys, function keys, control keys, navigation keys and modifier keys such as Shift, Ctrl and Alt.

notes_list.title: Mouse
notes_list.basic_overview: A mouse is a pointing input device used to move the pointer and perform actions such as clicking, selecting and dragging.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Modern mice commonly use optical or laser-based sensing instead of the mechanical ball mechanism used in older mice.

notes_list.title: Scanner
notes_list.basic_overview: A scanner converts physical documents or images into digital form.
notes_list.extra_info_content: OCR software can recognize printed characters in a scanned document and convert them into machine-readable text.

notes_list.title: OCR
notes_list.basic_overview: OCR stands for Optical Character Recognition and is used to identify printed or written characters from images and convert them into editable or searchable text.
notes_list.extra_info_content: OCR is especially useful for digitizing books, forms, scanned documents and printed records.

notes_list.title: OMR
notes_list.basic_overview: OMR stands for Optical Mark Recognition and detects marked responses on specially designed forms.
notes_list.extra_info_content: OMR is widely associated with objective examination answer sheets, surveys and forms containing marked bubbles or boxes.

notes_list.title: MICR
notes_list.basic_overview: MICR stands for Magnetic Ink Character Recognition and is used extensively in banking for processing characters printed with magnetic ink.
notes_list.extra_info_content: MICR technology is traditionally associated with cheque processing. Banking examinations frequently ask the full form and application of MICR.

notes_list.title: Monitor
notes_list.basic_overview: A monitor is an output device that displays visual information generated by a computer.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Common display technologies include LCD, LED-backlit LCD and OLED. Resolution describes the number of pixels available for displaying an image.

notes_list.title: Printer
notes_list.basic_overview: A printer produces a physical representation of digital information on paper or another medium.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Printers are broadly classified into impact and non-impact types. Dot-matrix is an impact printer, while inkjet and laser printers are non-impact printers.

notes_list.title: Plotter
notes_list.basic_overview: A plotter is an output device historically designed for producing large, precise drawings such as engineering plans, maps and architectural designs.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Modern large-format printers can perform many functions historically associated with plotters, but the term remains common in competitive-exam questions.

notes_list.title: RAM
notes_list.basic_overview: RAM stands for Random Access Memory and provides temporary working storage for programs and data currently being used by the system.
notes_list.extra_info_content: RAM is generally volatile memory, meaning its contents are lost when power is removed. DRAM and SRAM are important types of semiconductor memory.

notes_list.title: ROM
notes_list.basic_overview: ROM stands for Read-Only Memory and traditionally refers to non-volatile memory used to store information that should persist without power.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Modern systems use several forms of non-volatile memory. PROM, EPROM and EEPROM are classic ROM-family terms frequently asked in exams.

notes_list.title: Cache Memory
notes_list.basic_overview: Cache is high-speed memory used to store frequently accessed data and instructions so that the CPU can access them more quickly.
notes_list.extra_info_content: CPU caches are commonly organized into levels such as L1, L2 and L3. L1 is typically smaller and faster than higher-level caches.

notes_list.title: Hard Disk Drive
notes_list.basic_overview: HDD stands for Hard Disk Drive and stores data magnetically on rotating disks.
notes_list.extra_info_content: An HDD contains rotating platters and read/write heads. It is non-volatile storage and retains data after power is removed.

notes_list.title: Solid State Drive
notes_list.basic_overview: SSD stands for Solid State Drive and stores data using non-volatile flash memory rather than rotating magnetic disks.
notes_list.extra_info_content: SSDs generally have lower access latency and no mechanical moving parts. NVMe SSDs communicate through high-speed interfaces such as PCIe.

notes_list.title: Pen Drive
notes_list.basic_overview: A pen drive is a portable flash-memory storage device that commonly connects to a computer through USB.
notes_list.extra_info_content: It is non-volatile storage and can be used to transfer files between compatible devices.

notes_list.title: Optical Storage
notes_list.basic_overview: Optical storage uses laser technology to read and/or write data on optical discs such as CDs, DVDs and Blu-ray discs.
notes_list.extra_info_content: CD, DVD and Blu-ray differ in capacity and recording technology. Blu-ray generally provides substantially greater storage capacity than standard DVDs.

notes_list.title: Bit and Byte
notes_list.basic_overview: A bit is the smallest basic unit of digital information and can represent 0 or 1. A byte conventionally consists of 8 bits.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Common storage units include KB, MB, GB, TB, PB and beyond. In computing, powers of 2 are also used, with KiB = 1024 bytes, MiB = 1024 KiB and so on.

notes_list.title: Binary Number System
notes_list.basic_overview: The binary number system uses only two digits, 0 and 1, and is fundamental to digital computing.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Binary is base 2. Decimal is base 10, octal is base 8 and hexadecimal is base 16. Competitive exams frequently ask conversions among these number systems.

notes_list.title: System Software
notes_list.basic_overview: System software manages computer hardware and provides a platform for application software.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Operating systems, device drivers, language translators and certain utility programs are commonly classified as system software.

notes_list.title: Application Software
notes_list.basic_overview: Application software is designed to perform tasks for end users, such as word processing, spreadsheets, presentations and web browsing.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Examples include word processors, spreadsheet applications, presentation software, media players and web browsers.

notes_list.title: Utility Software
notes_list.basic_overview: Utility software performs maintenance, management, security or optimization functions for a computer system.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Examples include backup utilities, antivirus programs, file compression tools, disk management utilities and system monitoring tools.

notes_list.title: What is an Operating System?
notes_list.basic_overview: An operating system is system software that manages hardware resources and provides services and interfaces for applications and users.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Major OS responsibilities include process management, memory management, file management, device management, security and user interaction.

notes_list.title: Examples of Operating Systems
notes_list.basic_overview: Examples of operating systems include Microsoft Windows, Linux distributions, macOS, Android and iOS.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Linux is an operating-system kernel used in many distributions. Android is built around the Linux kernel with additional platform components.

notes_list.title: GUI and CLI
notes_list.basic_overview: GUI stands for Graphical User Interface, while CLI stands for Command-Line Interface.
notes_list.extra_info_content: GUI allows interaction through graphical elements such as windows, icons and menus. CLI allows users to issue commands through text.

notes_list.title: Multitasking
notes_list.basic_overview: Multitasking is the ability of an operating system to manage multiple tasks or processes so that users can work with several programs in a responsive environment.
notes_list.extra_info_content: On modern multi-core systems, multiple processes may execute simultaneously on different cores, while scheduling mechanisms manage processor time across runnable tasks.

notes_list.title: Machine Language
notes_list.basic_overview: Machine language consists of binary instructions that can be directly executed by a processor.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Machine language is hardware-dependent and is generally difficult for humans to read and write.

notes_list.title: Assembly Language
notes_list.basic_overview: Assembly language uses symbolic mnemonics to represent machine-level instructions and requires an assembler for translation into machine code.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Assembly language is generally processor-specific. Mnemonics such as MOV, ADD and SUB are commonly associated with assembly programming.

notes_list.title: High-Level Language
notes_list.basic_overview: High-level programming languages use abstractions and syntax designed to be easier for humans to understand than machine language.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Examples include C, C++, Java, Python, JavaScript and many other languages. Translation or interpretation ultimately allows their instructions to be executed by the computer.

notes_list.title: Compiler
notes_list.basic_overview: A compiler translates a program from a higher-level language into a lower-level representation such as machine code or an intermediate representation, depending on the language and implementation.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Traditional compiler models translate larger portions or the complete source program before execution. Modern language implementations may use multiple stages including compilation and runtime techniques.

notes_list.title: Interpreter
notes_list.basic_overview: An interpreter executes or translates program instructions at runtime rather than producing a conventional standalone machine-code executable in the traditional model.
notes_list.extra_info_content: The common exam shortcut that an interpreter always translates exactly one complete line at a time is an oversimplification. Real language runtimes can use parsing, bytecode, JIT compilation and other techniques.

notes_list.title: Assembler
notes_list.basic_overview: An assembler converts assembly language instructions into machine-level code or an equivalent object representation.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Remember the standard mapping: Assembly Language → Assembler; High-Level Language → Compiler/Interpreter depending on the language and implementation.

notes_list.title: Decimal Number System
notes_list.basic_overview: The decimal number system has base 10 and uses digits from 0 to 9.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Decimal is the conventional number system used in everyday arithmetic. In positional notation, each digit has a value determined by its position and powers of 10.

notes_list.title: Binary Number System
notes_list.basic_overview: The binary number system has base 2 and uses only 0 and 1.
notes_list.extra_info_content: A binary digit is called a bit. Digital circuits use two-state logic that naturally maps to binary representation.

notes_list.title: Octal Number System
notes_list.basic_overview: The octal number system has base 8 and uses digits 0 through 7.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Octal provides a compact representation of binary because each octal digit corresponds to three binary bits.

notes_list.title: Hexadecimal Number System
notes_list.basic_overview: The hexadecimal number system has base 16 and uses 0–9 and A–F as its digits.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Each hexadecimal digit corresponds to four binary bits. Hexadecimal is widely used in programming, memory addressing and digital representations.

notes_list.title: AND Gate
notes_list.basic_overview: An AND gate produces output 1 only when all of its inputs are 1.
notes_list.extra_info_content: For two inputs, AND follows: 0 AND 0 = 0, 0 AND 1 = 0, 1 AND 0 = 0 and 1 AND 1 = 1.

notes_list.title: OR Gate
notes_list.basic_overview: An OR gate produces output 1 when at least one input is 1.
notes_list.extra_info_content: For two inputs, only 0 OR 0 produces 0. All other input combinations produce 1.

notes_list.title: NOT Gate
notes_list.basic_overview: A NOT gate reverses the logical state of its input.
notes_list.extra_info_content: If the input is 0, the output is 1. If the input is 1, the output is 0. NOT is also called an inverter.

notes_list.title: NAND and NOR Gates
notes_list.basic_overview: NAND is the inverse of AND, while NOR is the inverse of OR. Both NAND and NOR are universal logic gates.
notes_list.extra_info_content: A universal gate can be used to construct other basic logic functions. Competitive exams frequently ask which gates are universal: NAND and NOR.

notes_list.title: XOR Gate
notes_list.basic_overview: An XOR gate produces output 1 when its inputs are different.
notes_list.extra_info_content: For two inputs, XOR gives 1 for 0,1 and 1,0; it gives 0 for 0,0 and 1,1.

notes_list.title: MS Word
notes_list.basic_overview: Microsoft Word is a word-processing application used to create, edit, format and print documents.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Common features include styles, spell checking, tables, headers and footers, page formatting, mail merge and document review tools.

notes_list.title: Mail Merge
notes_list.basic_overview: Mail Merge combines a main document with a data source to create multiple personalized documents such as letters, labels or envelopes.
notes_list.extra_info_content: A common example is generating personalized letters for many recipients from a single template and a list containing names and addresses.

notes_list.title: Find and Replace
notes_list.basic_overview: Find and Replace allows users to locate specified text and replace it with other text throughout a document.
notes_list.extra_info_content: The feature is useful for correcting repeated terms, changing names or updating formatting-related text efficiently.

notes_list.title: MS Excel
notes_list.basic_overview: Microsoft Excel is a spreadsheet application used for data entry, calculations, analysis, charts and reporting.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Excel organizes data into rows and columns. A cell is identified by a column label and row number, such as A1.

notes_list.title: Cell and Range
notes_list.basic_overview: A cell is the intersection of a row and column, while a range is a collection of selected cells.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Example: A1 is a single cell, while A1:C5 represents a rectangular range extending from A1 to C5.

notes_list.title: Excel Formula
notes_list.basic_overview: An Excel formula is an expression used to calculate a result and normally begins with an equals sign.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Examples include =SUM(A1:A5), =AVERAGE(B1:B5) and =MAX(C1:C10). Functions are predefined operations provided by Excel.

notes_list.title: Common Excel Functions
notes_list.basic_overview: Frequently used Excel functions include SUM, AVERAGE, COUNT, COUNTA, MAX, MIN, IF and ROUND.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Competitive exams may ask the purpose of functions. SUM adds values, AVERAGE calculates arithmetic mean, MAX returns the largest value and MIN returns the smallest.

notes_list.title: MS PowerPoint
notes_list.basic_overview: Microsoft PowerPoint is presentation software used to create slide-based presentations.
notes_list.extra_info_content: PowerPoint presentations can contain text, images, charts, tables, audio, video, animations and transitions.

notes_list.title: Slide Transition vs Animation
notes_list.basic_overview: A transition controls the visual effect when moving from one slide to another, while animation controls effects applied to objects within a slide.
notes_list.extra_info_content: This distinction is a common objective-question topic in computer awareness examinations.

notes_list.title: Ctrl + C
notes_list.basic_overview: Ctrl + C is commonly used to copy selected text, files or objects.
notes_list.extra_info_content: The copied content is placed on the clipboard and can normally be inserted using Ctrl + V.

notes_list.title: Ctrl + X
notes_list.basic_overview: Ctrl + X is commonly used to cut selected content.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Cut content is normally placed on the clipboard and can be pasted using Ctrl + V.

notes_list.title: Ctrl + V
notes_list.basic_overview: Ctrl + V is commonly used to paste clipboard content.
notes_list.extra_info_content: The exact result depends on the application and the type of content currently stored on the clipboard.

notes_list.title: Ctrl + Z
notes_list.basic_overview: Ctrl + Z commonly performs the Undo operation.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Undo reverses a recent action when the application supports undo history.

notes_list.title: Ctrl + Y
notes_list.basic_overview: Ctrl + Y commonly performs Redo or repeats the last action depending on the application.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Shortcut behavior can vary between applications, so exam questions should be interpreted in the context of standard Windows or Office conventions.

notes_list.title: Ctrl + A
notes_list.basic_overview: Ctrl + A commonly selects all available content in the current context.
notes_list.extra_info_content: In a document it may select all text; in a file-management window it can select all visible items.

notes_list.title: Ctrl + S
notes_list.basic_overview: Ctrl + S commonly saves the current document or file.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Using Save regularly reduces the risk of losing changes due to crashes or power interruptions.

notes_list.title: Ctrl + P
notes_list.basic_overview: Ctrl + P commonly opens the print interface for the current document or page.
notes_list.extra_info_content: The exact print dialog depends on the operating system and application.

notes_list.title: Ctrl + F
notes_list.basic_overview: Ctrl + F commonly opens a Find or Search function.
notes_list.extra_info_content: It is widely supported in browsers, documents, spreadsheets and many other applications.

notes_list.title: Alt + Tab
notes_list.basic_overview: Alt + Tab is commonly used in Windows to switch between open applications or windows.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Holding Alt while pressing Tab cycles through available windows in the standard Windows interface.

notes_list.title: Windows + D
notes_list.basic_overview: Windows + D commonly shows or hides the desktop.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Pressing the shortcut again can restore the previously visible windows in standard Windows behavior.

notes_list.title: Windows + L
notes_list.basic_overview: Windows + L locks the Windows computer.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Locking the computer protects the current session from unauthorized local access while keeping the session active.

notes_list.title: Alt + F4
notes_list.basic_overview: Alt + F4 commonly closes the active window or application.
notes_list.extra_info_content: If the active application has unsaved changes, it may display a prompt before closing.

notes_list.title: Internet
notes_list.basic_overview: The Internet is a global system of interconnected computer networks that communicate using standardized protocols.
notes_list.extra_info_content: The Internet supports services such as the World Wide Web, email, file transfer, streaming, online banking and many other applications.

notes_list.title: World Wide Web
notes_list.basic_overview: The World Wide Web is a system of interlinked web resources accessed over the Internet using web technologies and protocols.
notes_list.extra_info_content: The Web is not synonymous with the Internet. The Internet is the underlying global network infrastructure, while the Web is one major service that operates over it.

notes_list.title: URL
notes_list.basic_overview: URL stands for Uniform Resource Locator and identifies the location and access method of a resource on a network.
notes_list.extra_info_content: A typical URL can contain a scheme such as HTTPS, a domain name, a path and optional query or fragment components.

notes_list.title: IP Address
notes_list.basic_overview: An IP address is a numerical network address used to identify an interface or endpoint in an IP network.
notes_list.extra_info_content: IPv4 uses 32-bit addresses, while IPv6 uses 128-bit addresses. IPv6 was developed partly to address the limited address space of IPv4.

notes_list.title: HTTP and HTTPS
notes_list.basic_overview: HTTP is the Hypertext Transfer Protocol used for web communication, while HTTPS is HTTP protected using TLS encryption and authentication mechanisms.
notes_list.extra_info_content: HTTPS helps protect data in transit against interception and tampering and authenticates the server through digital certificates.

notes_list.title: FTP
notes_list.basic_overview: FTP stands for File Transfer Protocol and is designed for transferring files over a network.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Traditional FTP does not provide the same transport security as encrypted protocols such as SFTP or FTPS.

notes_list.title: SMTP
notes_list.basic_overview: SMTP stands for Simple Mail Transfer Protocol and is primarily used for sending email between mail systems and from clients to mail servers.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Receiving email commonly involves protocols such as POP3 or IMAP. SMTP is primarily associated with mail submission and transfer.

notes_list.title: POP3 and IMAP
notes_list.basic_overview: POP3 and IMAP are protocols used for retrieving or accessing email messages from mail servers.
notes_list.extra_info_content: POP3 traditionally downloads messages to a client, while IMAP is designed for synchronized access to messages stored on the mail server.

notes_list.title: DNS
notes_list.basic_overview: DNS stands for Domain Name System and translates domain names into IP addresses and other DNS records.
notes_list.extra_info_content: DNS allows users to access services using memorable names such as example.com instead of manually entering numerical IP addresses.

notes_list.title: Modem
notes_list.basic_overview: A modem is a device that performs modulation and demodulation or equivalent signal conversion functions to enable communication over certain communication links.
notes_list.extra_info_content: The traditional name modem comes from modulator-demodulator. Modern broadband equipment may combine modem, router and other networking functions.

notes_list.title: Router
notes_list.basic_overview: A router forwards packets between different networks using network-layer addressing and routing information.
notes_list.extra_info_content: A home router commonly connects a local network to an Internet service and may also provide DHCP, NAT, firewall and Wi-Fi functions.

notes_list.title: Switch
notes_list.basic_overview: A network switch connects devices within a local network and forwards Ethernet frames based on MAC addresses.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Compared with a traditional Ethernet hub, a switch can selectively forward frames to the relevant port instead of broadcasting every frame to all ports.

notes_list.title: Hub
notes_list.basic_overview: A hub is a basic networking device that repeats incoming signals to multiple ports.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Traditional Ethernet hubs operate at the physical layer and do not make forwarding decisions based on MAC addresses.

notes_list.title: Malware
notes_list.basic_overview: Malware is malicious software designed to disrupt, damage, abuse, spy on or gain unauthorized access to computer systems or data.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Common malware categories include viruses, worms, trojans, ransomware and spyware. Different malware types spread and operate in different ways.

notes_list.title: Computer Virus
notes_list.basic_overview: A computer virus is malicious code that typically attaches to a host file or program and replicates when the infected host is executed.
notes_list.extra_info_content: A virus generally requires some form of host or user execution for propagation, unlike a network worm that can spread independently across vulnerable systems.

notes_list.title: Computer Worm
notes_list.basic_overview: A computer worm is malware capable of self-replicating and spreading across networks without requiring a traditional host file.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Worms can consume network bandwidth and system resources and may exploit software vulnerabilities to spread.

notes_list.title: Trojan Horse
notes_list.basic_overview: A Trojan is malicious software that disguises itself as legitimate or useful software to trick users into executing it.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Unlike a traditional virus, a Trojan does not necessarily replicate itself. Its key characteristic is deceptive delivery or appearance.

notes_list.title: Ransomware
notes_list.basic_overview: Ransomware is malware that typically blocks access to systems or encrypts data and demands payment or another form of ransom.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Regular offline or otherwise protected backups are an important defense against data loss from ransomware. Paying ransom does not guarantee recovery.

notes_list.title: Spyware
notes_list.basic_overview: Spyware is software designed to monitor activities or collect information from a user or system without appropriate authorization.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Spyware can be used to collect browsing activity, credentials or other sensitive information depending on its capabilities.

notes_list.title: Phishing
notes_list.basic_overview: Phishing is a social-engineering technique in which attackers impersonate trustworthy entities to trick users into revealing sensitive information or performing harmful actions.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Phishing can occur through email, SMS, messaging apps, websites, phone calls and social media. Banking users should verify links, domains and requests for OTPs or credentials.

notes_list.title: Smishing
notes_list.basic_overview: Smishing is phishing conducted through SMS or text messaging.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Fake bank alerts, KYC warnings, prize messages and urgent payment requests are common social-engineering patterns.

notes_list.title: Vishing
notes_list.basic_overview: Vishing is phishing conducted through voice calls or other voice-based communication.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Attackers may impersonate bank staff, officials, customer-support agents or other trusted persons to obtain confidential information.

notes_list.title: Denial of Service
notes_list.basic_overview: A Denial-of-Service attack attempts to make a service or resource unavailable to legitimate users.
notes_list.extra_info_content: A Distributed Denial-of-Service attack uses multiple systems or sources to generate malicious traffic or requests.

notes_list.title: Strong Password
notes_list.basic_overview: A strong password is difficult to guess and should generally be long, unique and not reused across important accounts.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Password managers can help generate and store unique passwords. Multi-factor authentication provides an additional layer of protection.

notes_list.title: Two-Factor Authentication
notes_list.basic_overview: Two-factor authentication requires two distinct authentication factors, commonly something the user knows plus something the user possesses or is.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Examples include a password plus an authenticator-app code or security key. MFA is the broader term when two or more factors are used.

notes_list.title: Firewall
notes_list.basic_overview: A firewall controls or filters network traffic according to defined security rules.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Firewalls can be implemented in software, hardware or network infrastructure. They help restrict unauthorized network communication but are not a complete security solution.

notes_list.title: Antivirus
notes_list.basic_overview: Antivirus or anti-malware software detects, blocks and removes malicious software using techniques such as signatures, heuristics and behavioral analysis.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Security software should be kept updated because new malware and attack techniques continuously emerge.

notes_list.title: Database
notes_list.basic_overview: A database is an organized collection of data designed to facilitate storage, retrieval, management and analysis.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Databases are used in banking, railway reservations, education systems, government services, e-commerce and many other applications.

notes_list.title: DBMS
notes_list.basic_overview: DBMS stands for Database Management System and is software used to create, store, retrieve, update and manage databases.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Examples of database-management systems include MySQL, PostgreSQL, Oracle Database, Microsoft SQL Server and SQLite.

notes_list.title: RDBMS
notes_list.basic_overview: RDBMS stands for Relational Database Management System and organizes data primarily into related tables.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Rows generally represent records and columns represent attributes. Relationships between tables can be established using keys.

notes_list.title: Primary Key
notes_list.basic_overview: A primary key uniquely identifies each record in a relational table.
notes_list.extra_info_content: A primary key must uniquely identify rows and cannot contain NULL values in standard relational database design.

notes_list.title: Foreign Key
notes_list.basic_overview: A foreign key is a field or set of fields in one table that references a key in another table to establish a relationship.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Foreign keys help maintain referential integrity between related tables.

notes_list.title: SQL
notes_list.basic_overview: SQL stands for Structured Query Language and is widely used to interact with relational databases.
notes_list.extra_info_content: SQL can be used to retrieve, insert, update and delete data and to define or modify database structures, depending on the statement.

notes_list.title: SELECT Statement
notes_list.basic_overview: The SQL SELECT statement is used to retrieve data from one or more database tables or other queryable sources.
notes_list.extra_info_content: A basic query may look like SELECT column_name FROM table_name; Additional clauses such as WHERE, GROUP BY and ORDER BY can refine results.

notes_list.title: INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE
notes_list.basic_overview: INSERT adds records, UPDATE modifies existing records and DELETE removes records from a database table.
notes_list.extra_info_content: These commands are commonly classified under Data Manipulation Language. Always use appropriate WHERE conditions with UPDATE and DELETE operations to avoid unintended changes.

notes_list.title: Cloud Computing
notes_list.basic_overview: Cloud computing provides on-demand access to computing resources such as servers, storage, databases and software over a network, commonly the Internet.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Cloud services can reduce the need for organizations to maintain all computing infrastructure locally and can support scalable resource usage.

notes_list.title: IaaS, PaaS and SaaS
notes_list.basic_overview: IaaS provides infrastructure resources, PaaS provides a platform for application development and deployment, and SaaS delivers complete software applications as services.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Typical examples: IaaS provides virtual machines and storage; PaaS provides managed development/runtime environments; SaaS provides end-user applications through a service model.

notes_list.title: Public, Private and Hybrid Cloud
notes_list.basic_overview: Public cloud services are offered to multiple customers through shared provider infrastructure, private cloud environments are dedicated to a specific organization, and hybrid cloud combines multiple environments.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Cloud deployment models differ from service models. Public/private/hybrid describe deployment, while IaaS/PaaS/SaaS describe service abstraction.

notes_list.title: Artificial Intelligence
notes_list.basic_overview: Artificial Intelligence refers to computational systems designed to perform tasks that normally require aspects of human intelligence, such as perception, reasoning or language processing.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Machine learning is a major approach within AI in which systems learn patterns from data. Generative AI can produce text, images, audio, code and other content.

notes_list.title: Machine Learning
notes_list.basic_overview: Machine learning is a field of AI in which algorithms learn patterns or relationships from data to make predictions or decisions.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Common learning categories include supervised learning, unsupervised learning and reinforcement learning.

notes_list.title: Internet of Things
notes_list.basic_overview: IoT refers to interconnected physical devices equipped with sensors, software and network connectivity that can collect and exchange data.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Examples include smart meters, connected vehicles, industrial sensors, wearable devices and smart-home equipment.

notes_list.title: Blockchain
notes_list.basic_overview: Blockchain is a distributed ledger technology in which records are maintained through a network and linked using cryptographic techniques.
notes_list.extra_info_content: A blockchain can support tamper-evident records and decentralized verification. Cryptocurrencies are one application, but blockchain technology is broader than cryptocurrency.

notes_list.title: Big Data
notes_list.basic_overview: Big Data refers to datasets whose volume, velocity, variety or other characteristics create challenges for conventional data-processing approaches.
notes_list.extra_info_content: The commonly discussed 3Vs are Volume, Velocity and Variety. Additional Vs such as Veracity and Value are also used in different frameworks.

notes_list.title: UPI
notes_list.basic_overview: UPI stands for Unified Payments Interface and enables interoperable real-time digital payments between participating bank accounts through a common platform.
notes_list.extra_info_content: UPI is developed and operated within India's retail-payment ecosystem under the framework associated with NPCI. Users can make payments using UPI IDs, QR codes and other supported methods.

notes_list.title: IMPS
notes_list.basic_overview: IMPS stands for Immediate Payment Service and provides an electronic interbank fund-transfer facility available through participating channels.
notes_list.extra_info_content: IMPS is widely associated with immediate electronic fund transfers and is a common topic in Indian banking examinations.

notes_list.title: NEFT
notes_list.basic_overview: NEFT stands for National Electronic Funds Transfer and is an electronic funds-transfer system operated under the RBI framework.
notes_list.extra_info_content: NEFT facilitates electronic transfer of funds between participating bank accounts. It is different from RTGS and IMPS in its underlying processing and service characteristics.

notes_list.title: RTGS
notes_list.basic_overview: RTGS stands for Real Time Gross Settlement and settles eligible transactions individually in real time rather than netting them in batches.
notes_list.extra_info_content: RTGS is primarily associated with high-value fund transfers, although applicable minimum and maximum transaction rules are determined by the current system framework.

notes_list.title: ATM
notes_list.basic_overview: ATM stands for Automated Teller Machine and provides customers with self-service banking functions such as cash withdrawal and balance inquiry.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Depending on the machine and bank, ATMs can also support cash deposits, PIN changes, mini statements and other services.

notes_list.title: POS
notes_list.basic_overview: POS stands for Point of Sale and refers to the location or system where a customer transaction is completed.
notes_list.extra_info_content: In card-payment contexts, a POS terminal can read payment cards or accept supported contactless transactions.

notes_list.title: QR Code
notes_list.basic_overview: QR stands for Quick Response and refers to a two-dimensional barcode capable of storing machine-readable information.
notes_list.extra_info_content: QR codes are widely used in digital payments, authentication, ticketing, inventory systems and information sharing.

notes_list.title: CPU
notes_list.basic_overview: CPU = Central Processing Unit.
notes_list.extra_info_content: CPU is the primary processing component responsible for executing instructions and coordinating computational operations.

notes_list.title: RAM
notes_list.basic_overview: RAM = Random Access Memory.
notes_list.extra_info_content: RAM is commonly used as temporary working memory and is generally volatile.

notes_list.title: ROM
notes_list.basic_overview: ROM = Read-Only Memory.
notes_list.extra_info_content: ROM is traditionally associated with non-volatile storage of firmware or other persistent information.

notes_list.title: USB
notes_list.basic_overview: USB = Universal Serial Bus.
notes_list.extra_info_content: USB is a widely used standard for connecting peripherals and transferring data and power between compatible devices.

notes_list.title: GUI
notes_list.basic_overview: GUI = Graphical User Interface.
notes_list.extra_info_content: GUI provides visual interaction through elements such as windows, icons, menus and pointers.

notes_list.title: BIOS
notes_list.basic_overview: BIOS = Basic Input/Output System and refers to firmware traditionally used to initialize hardware and begin the boot process on compatible PCs.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Modern PCs commonly use UEFI firmware, although the term BIOS remains widely used in everyday and exam contexts.

notes_list.title: URL
notes_list.basic_overview: URL = Uniform Resource Locator.
notes_list.extra_info_content: A URL identifies the location and access method of a resource.

notes_list.title: HTTP
notes_list.basic_overview: HTTP = Hypertext Transfer Protocol.
notes_list.extra_info_content: HTTP is an application-layer protocol used for communication in the World Wide Web and other networked applications.

notes_list.title: HTTPS
notes_list.basic_overview: HTTPS = Hypertext Transfer Protocol Secure.
notes_list.extra_info_content: HTTPS uses TLS to provide encrypted and authenticated communication for HTTP connections.

notes_list.title: LAN, MAN and WAN
notes_list.basic_overview: LAN = Local Area Network, MAN = Metropolitan Area Network and WAN = Wide Area Network.
notes_list.extra_info_content: LAN generally covers a limited local area, MAN is associated with a metropolitan-scale area and WAN spans larger geographical regions.

notes_list.title: Internet vs WWW
notes_list.basic_overview: The Internet is the global network infrastructure, while the World Wide Web is a service that operates over the Internet.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Therefore, Internet and WWW are not interchangeable terms. Email, online gaming and many other services can use the Internet without being part of the Web.

notes_list.title: RAM vs ROM
notes_list.basic_overview: RAM is generally volatile working memory, while ROM traditionally refers to non-volatile memory used for persistent information.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Do not interpret 'Read-Only' as meaning every modern ROM-family device can never be rewritten. PROM, EPROM and EEPROM have different programming characteristics.

notes_list.title: Virus vs Worm
notes_list.basic_overview: A traditional virus generally depends on a host file or program, whereas a worm is designed to self-propagate across systems or networks.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Both are malware, but their propagation mechanisms differ.

notes_list.title: Compiler vs Interpreter
notes_list.basic_overview: A compiler generally translates source code into another representation before execution, while an interpreter executes or translates program constructs at runtime.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Modern language implementations can combine compilation, interpretation and just-in-time techniques, so simplistic one-line definitions are useful for basic exams but not complete descriptions of real runtimes.

notes_list.title: Hub vs Switch
notes_list.basic_overview: A hub repeats incoming signals to multiple ports, while a switch forwards Ethernet frames based on MAC-address information.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Traditional hubs operate at the physical layer, while standard Ethernet switches primarily operate at the data-link layer.

notes_list.title: Basic Computer Revision
notes_list.basic_overview: CPU processes instructions; RAM is working memory; ROM is traditionally non-volatile; keyboard and mouse are input devices; monitor and printer are output devices.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Remember the basic flow: Input → Processing → Output, with storage and communication supporting the system.

notes_list.title: Memory Revision
notes_list.basic_overview: Bit is a binary digit; byte is 8 bits; RAM is generally volatile; cache is high-speed memory close to the CPU; HDD and SSD are secondary storage devices.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Exam questions often ask which memory is fastest, which is volatile and which device is used for permanent storage.

notes_list.title: Internet Revision
notes_list.basic_overview: DNS resolves domain names; HTTP/HTTPS are web protocols; SMTP is used for sending mail; POP3 and IMAP are used for email retrieval/access; IP identifies network endpoints.
notes_list.extra_info_content: A common exam trap is confusing SMTP with POP3 or IMAP. SMTP is primarily associated with sending and transferring email.

notes_list.title: Cyber Security Revision
notes_list.basic_overview: Virus, worm, Trojan, ransomware and spyware are malware categories; phishing is social engineering; firewall filters network traffic; MFA adds authentication protection.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Never share passwords, PINs, CVV or OTPs in response to unsolicited calls, messages or links. Verify the source independently.

notes_list.title: Banking Computer Revision
notes_list.basic_overview: UPI enables interoperable instant digital payments; IMPS provides immediate electronic transfers; NEFT is an electronic funds-transfer system; RTGS settles eligible transactions individually in real time.
notes_list.extra_info_content: For banking exams, memorize the full forms and distinguish the basic purpose of UPI, IMPS, NEFT and RTGS.

notes_list.title: Important Shortcut Revision
notes_list.basic_overview: Ctrl+C = Copy; Ctrl+X = Cut; Ctrl+V = Paste; Ctrl+Z = Undo; Ctrl+Y = Redo/Repeat; Ctrl+A = Select All; Ctrl+S = Save; Ctrl+P = Print; Ctrl+F = Find.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Windows shortcuts frequently asked in exams include Alt+Tab for switching windows, Windows+L for locking the computer and Alt+F4 for closing the active window.
